titleEn: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat
author: Oliver Sacks
introFa: کتاب «The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat» نوشته Oliver Sacks یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

The 1966 meeting of the American Psychopath- ological Association was devoted to schizophre- nia and, like most symposia in the United States at the time, concentrated on psychopathological inquiries and speculations. Twenty years later the same body returned to the subject but, as these proceedings make clear, with a very different set of priorities. The writings of Kraepelin and Bleuler overshadowed many of the papers; Freud's name was never mentioned; the buzz topics were biological research, cognitive and phenomenological investigations and the role of psychosocial influences on outcome. No new insights emerge, but the book is given a touch of distinction by the inclusion of an award address by the veteran psychologist, Joseph Zubin, who has been a central figure in the Association for forty years and has edited many of its volumes. He would surely have tightened up the editorial reins on this occasion, for few readers will relish comments like 'I'm not hearing you. I think you'd be better off without the microphone', or even 'It would be a terrific asset to have you in town. That was a wonderful presentation.' students, for whom it adds little to the readily available glut of textbooks and review-articles. Migraine. By O. Sacks. (Pp. 270; illustrated; £14.95.) Duckworth: London. 1986. The Man Who Mistook His Wife For a Hat. By O. Sacks. (Pp. 233; illustrated; £9.95.) Duck- worth: London. 1985. The author of these two books is a British-trained, American-based neurologist with a gift for turning case-histories into short stories. At the heart of the revised edition of his book on migraine, published originally in 1971, is a battery of clinical vignettes round which he presents a reliable account of the history, causes, phenomenology and treatment of the syndromes, aimed explicitly at migrainous patients and ' general readers of a speculative turn of mind' as well as physicians. All the twenty-four chapters in the other volume are based on patients with uncommon functional disorders of the central nervous system. Some of them have already appeared in literary journals, as may be gathered from their titles, e.g. 'The man who mistook his wife for a hat' (a case of prosopagnosia) and 'Witty Ticcy Ray' (a case of Tourette's disease). In brief, belletristic neurology in the tradition of romantic medicine. Contemporary Issues in Schizophrenia. Edited by A. Kerr and P. Snaith. (Pp. 483; illustrated; £17.50.) Gaskell (Royal College of Psychia- trists): London. 1986. This volume, published under the aegis of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, contains forty- seven articles on schizophrenia, two thirds of them having appeared in the British Journal of Psychiatry over the past decade. The remainder comprises a group of commissioned overviews distributed among the seven sections into which the material is subdivided: general and historical, classification and phenomenology, organic, gen- etic, social, treatment and outcome. In view of the vast literature on the subject such an enterprise might be justified if striking advances had been established and most of them had been published in the journal concerned. Since neither of these conditions apply, the book must be aimed principally at postgraduate examination Psychopharmacology and Food. Edited by M. Sandier and T. Silverstone. Though the British Association for Psychophar- macology continues to entitle its publications 'monographs' they are in fact polygraphic proceedings of annual meetings. The first of these two volumes contains eleven papers dealing with the physiology, pharmacoloy and some clinical aspects of feeding and its disorders. Sound enough, but little more. The second, bumper volume is designed to provide an overview of psychopharmacology as a whole.
